key_terms.meaning: A computer running an Ethereum client that stores chain state and validates blocks and transactions
An account controlled by a private key, with no code, identified by a 20-byte address
An account that holds bytecode and storage and acts only when a transaction or message calls it
The native currency of Ethereum, used to pay gas and to transfer value between accounts
A balance recorded inside a contract's storage; it is not native currency and needs the contract to move
A signed instruction from an EOA that changes state once it is included in a block
An internal call from one contract to another during execution; it is not separately signed
A unit that measures computational work; gas used × gas price = fee paid in ether
A deterministic stack machine with 256-bit words that runs contract bytecode on every node
The EVM instruction stream produced by compiling a contract's source code
Code plus persistent storage on the blockchain that runs the same way for every node when called
A statically typed language with C-like syntax that compiles to EVM bytecode
A reusable guard in Solidity that checks a condition before or after a function body runs
A public Ethereum network with worthless coins used to test contracts before mainnet
A JSON file that defines the first block, chain ID and initial balances of a private network
The library object that sends JSON-RPC requests from a DApp to an Ethereum node
A JSON description of a contract's functions and arguments used to encode and decode calls
The first 4 bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of a function signature, placed at the start of call data
An organization whose rules, funds and decisions live in contracts and are driven by token voting
Greedy Heaviest Observed SubTree: the fork rule that follows the subtree with the most total work, not just the longest chain
A separate chain linked to a main chain by a bridge, with its own consensus and its own security

takeaways: Ethereum is an account-based blockchain: state is a mapping from addresses to balances, code and storage, and nodes agree on that state block by block.
Ether is the native coin; tokens are just numbers kept inside a contract, so holding a token never means holding ether.
A transaction is signed outside the chain and changes state once; a message is a nested call made while that transaction executes.
The EVM is a deterministic, gas-metered stack machine, which is why every node reaches the same state after running the same bytecode.
Gas turns computation into a price, so an infinite loop costs money instead of freezing the network.
A smart contract cannot act by itself: it only runs when a transaction or another contract calls it.
Solidity compiles to bytecode and an ABI, and the ABI is what lets a DApp talk to the deployed code.
Testnets and private nets exist so bugs are paid for with worthless coins, not real rupees.
GHOST and side chains are both answers to scaling: one changes how forks are chosen, the other moves work to a separate chain with its own security.
A DAO replaces managers with contracts and voting, so a bug in the voting rule is a bug in the organization.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit usually ask you to describe Ethereum's architecture or the EVM, then compare it with Bitcoin, then explain smart contracts, Solidity and DAOs with a concrete example.

bank.q: Draw and explain the components of the Ethereum ecosystem and the role each plays.
outline: Nodes and clients (execution client, consensus client)
Accounts: EOA and contract account
Wallets and key management
Ether, tokens and token standards
Developer tools: compilers, frameworks, testnets
DApps and block explorers built on top

bank.q: Distinguish between a transaction and a message, and between ether and a token.
outline: Transaction: signed by an EOA, changes state, costs gas, has nonce, to, value, data
Message: internal call from contract to contract, carries data and gas, not separately signed
Ether: native balance maintained by the protocol
Token: balance kept in a contract's storage, moved only by calling the contract
Consequence: sending a token needs a transaction to the token contract, not to the receiver

bank.q: Explain the Ethereum Virtual Machine as a stack machine and describe the role of gas in it.
outline: EVM is a virtual machine run by every node
256-bit words, stack-based, with memory and persistent storage
Bytecode is the instruction set: PUSH, ADD, SSTORE, CALL and so on
Deterministic: same input, same output on every node
Gas as a per-instruction cost, gas limit and gas price
Out-of-gas reverts state; fees go to the block proposer and partly burnt

bank.q: Define a smart contract and explain how it is deployed and invoked on Ethereum.
outline: Definition: code plus storage at an address
Deployment is a transaction with no recipient and bytecode as data
Constructor runs once, runtime code is stored, a contract address is produced
Invocation by a transaction whose data names a function and carries arguments
Every full node executes the call and agrees on the new state
Cannot run on its own; it needs a caller and gas

bank.q: What are the main features of Solidity, and how does source code become something the EVM can run?
outline: Statically typed, C-like syntax, contract-oriented
State variables, functions, events, modifiers, inheritance
Visibility and access rules: public, private, internal, external
Compilation produces bytecode and the ABI
Deployment puts bytecode on chain; the ABI stays off chain for tooling

bank.q: Why do developers use test networks? Describe setting up a private network and starting it.
outline: Mainnet mistakes cost real ether and cannot be undone
Public testnets: free coins from faucets, same client software
Private net: choose chain ID and network ID, write a genesis file
Initialise the data directory with the genesis file
Start the node with the same datadir and network ID
Attach a console, create accounts, start mining or use a dev consensus

bank.q: Write a Solidity contract for a simple escrow between a buyer and a seller with an arbiter, and explain who can call each function.
outline: State: addresses of buyer, seller, arbiter; amount; flags
Constructor sets parties and requires the deposit
release() callable only by buyer or arbiter, pays seller
refund() callable only by arbiter or seller, returns funds to buyer
Events emitted for release and refund
Access checks with require and modifiers; note that the contract cannot start itself

bank.q: Describe, step by step, how you would compile, test and deploy a contract using a development framework, and how the front end then calls it.
outline: Initialise the project and add the compiler plugin
Write the contract; add a test file using local accounts
Run the test suite on a local in-process chain
Configure the network endpoint and a signer key
Run the deploy script; deployment is a signed transaction
Save address and ABI; front end creates a provider and a contract object with that ABI and address
Calls read functions for free; write functions need a signer and gas

bank.q: Explain how a contract call is encoded, using the terms ABI, bytecode and function selector.
outline: ABI lists function names and argument types
Signature like transfer(address,uint256) is hashed with Keccak-256
First 4 bytes form the selector
Call data = selector followed by 32-byte padded arguments
The EVM jumps to the matching function in the bytecode
Return data is decoded using the ABI

bank.q: You must move a lottery contract from a testnet to mainnet. List the checks you would perform and the risks you would cover.
outline: Re-run the full test suite, including edge cases and reverts
Check randomness source: block values are predictable, prefer a commit-reveal or oracle
Review access control and payout logic
Estimate gas and set limits; keep a buffer for gas price change
Audit and, if possible, a bug bounty or a pause switch
Deploy, verify source on a block explorer, then fund gradually

bank.q: Compare GHOST with the longest-chain rule and explain why GHOST suits Ethereum's block times.
outline: Longest chain: picks the chain with most blocks, ignores side branches
Ghost: picks the subtree with the greatest total work, counting stale blocks
Short block times create many near-simultaneous blocks and frequent forks
Without GHOST, stale blocks waste work and unfairly cut rewards
GHOST keeps security in the heaviest subtree and credits stale blocks
Trade-off: more bookkeeping, different confirmation intuition

bank.q: Explain how a DAO works on Ethereum and evaluate its main risks.
outline: Membership and voting power held as tokens
Proposals submitted, debated and voted on chain
Treasury held by the contract and released only on a passed proposal
Execution automatic, so rules must be precise
Risks: code bugs, low turnout, vote buying, flash-loan voting, majority capture
Mitigations: timelocks, quorum, audit, upgrade or exit mechanisms

bank.q: Assess side chains as a scaling answer for Ethereum: what they gain and what they give up.
outline: Gain: higher throughput, lower fees, own consensus tuned for the use case
Bridge mechanism moves assets in and out
Give up: mainnet security does not extend to the side chain
Bridge becomes a large target; validator set may be small
Withdrawal delays and fraud or validity proofs add complexity
Reasonable for experiments and games, weaker for high-value settlement

bank.q: Compare Bitcoin and Ethereum in data model, execution, currency and consensus, and say what each design favours.
outline: Bitcoin: UTXO set, script with limited operations, 21 million cap, proof of work
Ethereum: accounts with balance, code and storage, Turing-complete EVM, no fixed cap but fee burn
Transactions: Bitcoin inputs and outputs; Ethereum nonce, to, value, data, gas fields
Contracts: Bitcoin script is a spending condition; Ethereum contracts hold state and call each other
Consensus: both began with proof of work; Ethereum moved to proof of stake
Design aim: Bitcoin favours simple, auditable value transfer; Ethereum favours general computation

glossary.def: A public, permissionless, account-based blockchain whose nodes run the EVM and agree on one shared state.
Software such as a full node implementation that stores the chain, validates blocks and answers RPC requests.
A counter on an externally owned account that increases with each outgoing transaction and blocks replay.
The maximum gas a sender allows a transaction to consume.
The amount of ether offered per unit of gas, which sets the fee when multiplied by gas used.
The smallest unit of ether; 1 ether = 10¹⁸ wei.
The binary instruction sequence the EVM executes for a contract.
A contract's permanent key-value store on chain, where every slot is 32 bytes.
A contract's temporary byte array, cleared after each external call.
An EVM operation that undoes state changes in the current call and returns the unused gas.
A log entry a contract writes during execution; it is stored in transaction receipts and read by off-chain tools.
A Solidity guard attached to a function that runs a check before or after the function body.
A widely used token interface standard with functions like transfer, balanceOf and approve.
A JSON description of a contract's functions and arguments, used to encode calls and decode results.
The first 4 bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of a function signature, used to identify the function in call data.
The request format a wallet or DApp uses to talk to an Ethereum node over HTTP or WebSocket.
The object that holds a private key or asks a wallet to sign a transaction before it is sent.
A public Ethereum network that uses worthless coins so contracts can be tested safely.
A service that sends small amounts of test ether to a testnet address.
The first block of a chain, defined by a configuration file for private networks.
An organization whose membership, treasury and decisions are governed by contracts and token voting.
A fork-choice rule that follows the subtree containing the most total work, counting stale blocks.
A valid block that is not on the chosen chain and earns no full reward.
An independent chain connected to a main chain by a bridge, with its own consensus and security.
